sine-cosine-tangent-s1.title: An angle $\theta$ on the unit circle
sine-cosine-tangent-s1.text: The angle $\theta$, with $0 < \theta < 2\pi$, is in standard position. Its terminal ray meets the unit circle at $P\left(-\frac{3}{5}, \frac{4}{5}\right)$.

sine-cosine-tangent-s2.title: A turning bicycle wheel
sine-cosine-tangent-s2.text: A bicycle wheel has radius 30 cm. A reflector on the rim starts on the positive $x$-axis of a coordinate system centered at the wheel's hub, and the wheel turns counterclockwise. The table gives the distance the reflector has traveled along the rim.

table.caption: Distance $s(t)$ traveled along the rim, in centimeters, $t$ seconds after the start

options: This drops the sign of the $x$-coordinate and uses it for sine; sine is the $y$-coordinate.

mistakes.why: $P$ is left of the $y$-axis, so its $x$-coordinate, $\cos\theta$, is negative.
That is the $y$-coordinate, $\sin\theta$. Cosine is the $x$-coordinate.
That is $\frac{x}{y}$. Tangent is the slope of the terminal ray, $\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \frac{y}{x}$.
The ray goes up to the left, so its slope is negative: $\frac{4/5}{-3/5} = -\frac{4}{3}$.

why.correct: $\tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \frac{4/5}{-3/5} = -\frac{4}{3}$, the slope of the ray from the origin to $P$.
$P$ has a negative $x$-coordinate and a positive $y$-coordinate, so it is in Quadrant II, between $\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\pi$.
options: In Quadrant I both coordinates are positive, but $P$ has $x < 0$.
In Quadrant III both coordinates are negative, but $P$ has $y > 0$.
In Quadrant IV, $x > 0$ and $y < 0$: the opposite of $P$'s signs.

why.correct: Turning another $\pi$ (half a turn) sends $P$ to the opposite point on the circle, $\left(\frac{3}{5}, -\frac{4}{5}\right)$. Its $y$-coordinate is $-\frac{4}{5}$.
options: Half a turn flips both coordinates' signs, so the height becomes $-\frac{4}{5}$.
$\frac{4}{5}$ would be $\sin(\theta + 2\pi)$: a full turn, back to $P$.

items.q: Through what angle, in radians, has the wheel turned at $t = 2$ seconds?

mistakes.why: That is the arc length in centimeters. Divide by the radius: $\theta = \frac{s}{r}$.
That divides the radius by the arc. Radian measure is arc over radius: $\frac{90}{30}$.

items.q: At $t = 2$, where is the reflector relative to the hub?
options: Left of the hub and above it (Quadrant II)
Right of the hub and above it (Quadrant I)
Left of the hub and below it (Quadrant III)
Right of the hub and below it (Quadrant IV)

why.correct: The angle is 3 radians. Since $\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57 < 3 < \pi \approx 3.14$, the terminal ray is in Quadrant II.
options: Quadrant I would need an angle below $\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57$.
Quadrant III starts at $\pi \approx 3.14$, just past 3.
Quadrant IV needs an angle between $\frac{3\pi}{2} \approx 4.71$ and $2\pi$; this reads 3 as degrees or miscounts the quarter turns.

items.q: The wheel keeps turning at the same rate. At what time $t$, in seconds, does the reflector first get back to its starting point?

mistakes.why: That is the angle of a full turn in radians, not the time. The rim distance of a full turn is $2\pi(30) = 60\pi$ cm, at 45 cm per second.
That treats a full turn as 360 cm. The circumference is $2\pi r = 60\pi$ cm.

why.correct: A full turn is $2\pi$ radians, or $2\pi(30) = 60\pi$ cm along the rim. At 45 cm per second this takes $\frac{60\pi}{45} = \frac{4\pi}{3}$ seconds, about 4.19 seconds.

items.q: Let $\theta$ be the angle the wheel has turned at $t = 3$. Which is true?

why.correct: $\theta = \frac{135}{30} = 4.5$ radians, between $\pi \approx 3.14$ and $\frac{3\pi}{2} \approx 4.71$: Quadrant III, where both coordinates are negative.
options: Quadrant III: left of and below the hub.
These are the Quadrant II signs, where the reflector was at $t = 2$.
These are the Quadrant IV signs; 4.5 is still less than $\frac{3\pi}{2} \approx 4.71$.
These are the Quadrant I signs, for angles below $\frac{\pi}{2}$.

mistakes.why: That is the conversion factor upside down. Multiply by $\frac{\pi}{180}$: $\frac{150\pi}{180} = \frac{5\pi}{6}$.
That uses $\pi$ radians $= 90^\circ$. Half a turn, $180^\circ$, is $\pi$ radians.
That uses $\pi = 360^\circ$. Half a turn is $\pi$, so $\pi$ radians $= 180^\circ$.

why.correct: $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ is three quarters of a turn, ending at $(0, -1)$. Its $y$-coordinate is $-1$.
options: The point is $(0, -1)$, so the height is $-1$.
$1$ is $\sin\frac{\pi}{2}$, at the top of the circle.
Sine is a coordinate on the unit circle, so it is never larger than 1; the angle is not the output.

items.q: The terminal ray of an angle $\theta$ in standard position passes through the point $(-2, 6)$. What is $\tan\theta$?

why.correct: $\tan\theta$ is the slope of the terminal ray, which goes through $(0, 0)$ and $(-2, 6)$: $\frac{6 - 0}{-2 - 0} = -3$. The point does not have to be on the unit circle.
options: This is run over rise; slope is rise over run.
The run is $-2$, so the slope is negative.
This uses only the $y$-coordinate. Tangent divides it by the $x$-coordinate.

items.q: Which angles have the same terminal ray as $\frac{\pi}{3}$? Select all that apply.

why.correct: Angles that differ by a multiple of $2\pi$ share a terminal ray: $\frac{\pi}{3} + 2\pi = \frac{7\pi}{3}$ and $\frac{\pi}{3} - 2\pi = -\frac{5\pi}{3}$.
options: This differs by $\pi$, half a turn, so its ray points the opposite way.
This is the mirror image across the $y$-axis, in Quadrant II.

why.correct: At $\frac{\pi}{2}$ the point is $(0, 1)$: $\cos\theta = 0$, so $\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ divides by zero. The terminal ray is vertical and has no slope.
options: At $\pi$ the ray is horizontal: $\tan\pi = \frac{0}{-1} = 0$, which is defined.

items.q: The angle $\theta$ increases from $0$ to $\frac{\pi}{2}$ and the point $P$ moves along the unit circle. Predict each change.

variables.name: $\sin\theta$
variables.why: The point climbs from the $x$-axis to the top of the circle, so its height goes from 0 up to 1.

variables.name: $\cos\theta$
variables.why: The point moves left from $x = 1$ toward the $y$-axis, so its $x$-coordinate drops from 1 to 0.

variables.name: The distance from $P$ to the origin
variables.why: Every point of the unit circle is 1 unit from the center, so this distance stays 1.

why.correct: In Quadrant I, turning counterclockwise raises the point and moves it left, always on the circle of radius 1.
